title: The time is uncertain
hook: 'i don't know' feels like failing a test; a weaver's daughter said it to the Buddha, and he praised her
tomorrow: why would anyone call waking up in the morning a wonder?

segments.voice: Last time, the week closed with the herons and the moon: time passes, and waking up late still lights the world. Now Atisha's second root, in a story.

Saying I don't know in class can feel like failing out loud. Now a crowd in the town of Alavi, gathered around the Buddha. A young weaver's daughter slips in late, and he speaks to her, in front of everyone. Where have you come from? I don't know. Where are you going? I don't know. Don't you know? I know. Do you know? I don't know. The crowd mutters. She's being rude to the Teacher. But the Buddha says: well answered.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW, OUT LOUD.` → `FOUR QUESTIONS IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` → `WELL ANSWERED?`

segments.voice: The story is told in the old commentary on the Dhammapada. The Buddha asks her to explain, and she does. Where have I come from? I don't know which life I came from. Where am I going? I don't know where I'll be born next. Don't I know? I know that I will die. Do I know? I don't know when. Every answer was exact. The commentary says she had taken the Buddha's teaching on death to heart when he'd visited before, and kept it up, so his questions landed on someone already listening. And there's a hard turn, said gently. The commentary says that same day, she died in an accident at her father's loom. She had been right: she didn't know when. That's the second of Atisha's three roots: the time of death is uncertain. Teachers who hand it down add that a lifespan isn't fixed, that the young can go before the old, and that no calendar has the date. It isn't there to scare anyone. It works on the sneaky thought under all our postponing: sure, I'll die, but not soon. The weaver's daughter didn't claim to know more than she did. She held one thing certain and one thing open, and lived between them, listening. No one knows when. So the kind word, the practice, the visit, doesn't wait for a date.
screen: `WHERE FROM? WHERE TO?` · `I KNOW I WILL DIE.` · `I DON'T KNOW WHEN.` · `THE SECOND ROOT: UNCERTAIN TIME.` · then, large: `NO ONE KNOWS WHEN.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound around you: a car, the fridge, a bird, a voice in another room. Notice you didn't know it was coming, and you can't say when it will stop. Rest with that sound and the second root together: no one knows when.
The time is uncertain: Atisha's second root. Death is sure; its hour isn't, for anyone.
Hold onto this: no one knows when, so the kind word doesn't wait for a date. Day sixteen thirty-two, well answered.

howItsDone: The weaver's daughter is a well-known story in Theravada teaching on mindfulness of death; in Tibetan Buddhism, the uncertainty of the time of death is the second root of the death contemplation taught near the start of the lamrim.

fork.setup: the Buddha asks you, in front of a crowd, 'do you know when you'll die?' everyone is listening. what does the weaver's daughter say?
options: 'not for many years, i hope; i'm young and healthy.'
fork.reveal: she held one thing certain, that she would die, and one thing open, when. the Buddha praised her answer.

original.note: Pali: impermanent, not lasting; why no one can know the hour.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'i don't know' means you weren't paying attention.
what it means: she knew she would die and didn't know when, and said exactly that; the second root asks the same honesty.
what a scholar hears: the story of the weaver's daughter is from the Dhammapada commentary on verse 174; the uncertainty of the time of death is Atisha's second root in the lamrim.
guess: death is certain, but its hour is unknown
the future is too unclear to make any plans
a teacher who isn't sure of his own answers
recall: Death comes even if we haven't practiced

chat.says: ông is older than bác Hùng was. i keep thinking, what if he's next?
options: No one knows when. So don't wait: tell him the thing this week.
He's healthy, so you've got years. No need to worry yet.
Try not to think about it. The not knowing only hurts.
chat.meaning: The second root: death is sure, its hour unknown, for anyone. That's not a reason for dread; it's a reason not to wait.

tie.story: The weaver's daughter told the Buddha she knew she would die but not when, and he said well answered.
tie.friend: Mai can't know when ông will die, so she can say what matters to him now.
tie.you: what kind word have you been saving for later?

Alavi.meaning: a town where the Buddha taught

Atisha.meaning: an Indian Buddhist teacher whose teachings shaped Tibetan practice

Dhammapada.meaning: a short collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

sources.ref: Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada-atthakatha) on verse 174: the story of the weaver's daughter of Alavi
Atisha's second root (the time of death is uncertain), as taught in the Tibetan lamrim

notes: Weaver's daughter (Dhp-a on verse 174) paraphrased. The commentary gives a number of years of practice between the Buddha's visits; omitted (claims rule). Her accidental death at her father's loom is told in one gentle line. Gentle note for parents: a sudden death in the story.
The order of the four questions follows the commonly retold version (where from, where to, don't you know, do you know); confirm against the commentary.
The supporting points of the second root (lifespan not fixed; young before old) are framed as what teachers add, per the lamrim presentation.
Story shape: told from the middle of the scene; the hook ends on the cliffhanger ('well answered?') and the teach solves it.
